nameStory: The American Herring Gull gets its name from its historical association with herring fishing areas, where these opportunistic birds would gather to feast on fish scraps and offal from fishing boats. The 'American' part distinguishes it from its European cousin, the Herring Gull, though scientists debate whether they're separate species or subspecies of the same bird.
description: The American Herring Gull is the classic 'seagull' that most New Englanders know and love (or love to hate). These robust, medium-to-large gulls are the quintessential coastal bird, with crisp white bodies, pearl-gray wings, and bright pink legs that look almost cartoonish. Adults reach about the size of a small chicken, with wingspans that can stretch nearly five feet across, making them one of our most noticeable shore birds.

idTips.label: Wing Pattern
idTips.description: Look for gray wings with distinctive black wingtips marked by bright white spots that look like someone dabbed them with correction fluid - these 'mirrors' flash conspicuously in flight

idTips.label: Bill Color
idTips.description: Adults sport a sturdy yellow bill with a prominent red spot on the lower mandible that looks like a drop of nail polish - chicks instinctively peck at this spot to trigger feeding

idTips.label: Leg Color
idTips.description: Bright pink or flesh-colored legs that stand out against rocky shores and sandy beaches, often looking almost neon in bright sunlight

idTips.label: Call
idTips.description: Their harsh 'kyow-kyow-kyow' call carries far over crashing waves and sounds like a rusty gate hinge mixed with laughter - once heard, never forgotten

idTips.label: Juvenile Appearance
idTips.description: Young birds look completely different - mottled brown and gray all over like a weather-beaten piece of driftwood, taking up to four years to develop full adult plumage

habitat: American Herring Gulls thrive wherever water meets opportunity throughout New England - from rocky Maine coastlines and sandy Cape Cod beaches to inland lakes, rivers, and reservoirs. You'll also spot them in decidedly un-nautical places like shopping mall parking lots, fast-food restaurants, and garbage dumps, where they've mastered the art of urban scavenging. They're equally at home on a remote island or strutting through a busy harbor town looking for handouts.

seasonality.spring: Adults return to breeding colonies with bright, clean plumage and begin their raucous courtship displays. Look for pairs performing 'bread-tossing' rituals where they regurgitate food for each other.
seasonality.summer: Peak nesting season finds them fiercely territorial around colonies, dive-bombing anyone who gets too close to their ground nests. Fluffy gray chicks begin appearing in early summer.
seasonality.fall: Mixed flocks of adults and confusing brown juveniles gather at beaches and landfills. Adults start showing more wear in their plumage as they molt.
seasonality.winter: Many remain year-round in New England, gathering in large flocks at fish processing plants, harbors, and anywhere food scraps are available. Their calls echo hauntingly across frozen harbors.

funFact: Herring Gulls are tool users - they've been observed dropping clams and sea urchins from great heights onto rocks to crack them open, and some have learned to steal food by pulling fishing lines up hand-over-hand (or rather, beak-over-foot) like feathered pirates.
confusionNotes: Most often confused with Ring-billed Gulls, but Herring Gulls are noticeably larger with pink (not yellow) legs and that red spot on the bill instead of a black ring. Remember: 'Ring-billed has a ring, Herring has a red dot.' Great Black-backed Gulls are much larger with dark gray (nearly black) backs rather than the Herring's pale gray.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'seagulls,' these birds aren't limited to seas at all and many live their entire lives around freshwater. The term 'seagull' isn't used by scientists - they're simply 'gulls' whether they live by oceans, lakes, or landfills.
compareHints: Among New England's large gulls, American Herring Gulls are the 'Goldilocks' species - not as massive as Great Black-backed Gulls, not as small as Ring-billed Gulls, but just right in the middle. Their pale gray backs are lighter than Great Black-backed Gulls but darker than Iceland Gulls, and their pink legs distinguish them from the yellow-legged Ring-billed and Lesser Black-backed Gulls.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Ring-billed Gulls are smaller and more delicate than Herring Gulls, lacking the Herring Gull's robust build and pink legs.

Among New England gulls, Great Black-backed Gulls dwarf the common Herring Gull in size and have much darker backs, while Ring-billed Gulls are significantly smaller with lighter grey backs and distinctive black rings around their bills.
Among New England's large gulls, Iceland Gulls are unique for their combination of medium size and extremely pale wing tips.
Among the large white-headed gulls, Lesser Black-backed Gulls are distinguished by their uniquely dark backs - darker than Herring Gulls but not as massive as Great Black-backed Gulls.
Among New England's large gulls, Glaucous Gulls stand out for their pale wingtips—Herring Gulls and Great Black-backed Gulls both have bold black wingtips, while Ring-billed Gulls are much smaller.
Common Gulls are smaller and more delicate than Herring Gulls, with yellow-green (not orange-red) bills and legs, plus a gentler facial expression.
Compared to the common Herring Gull, the Slaty-backed Gull has a noticeably darker slate-gray back and is generally larger and more robust.
Unlike Ring-billed Gulls which have a black ring on a yellow bill, Black-tailed Gulls have a red spot and often a black band near the bill tip.
Compared to the common Ring-billed Gull, Short-billed Gulls are smaller with cleaner wing tips and lack any dark markings on the bill.
Among the large white-headed gulls in its genus, the California Gull is most similar to the Ring-billed and Herring Gulls but sits between them in size.
Unlike the common white-bodied gulls of New England like Herring and Ring-billed Gulls, Heermann's Gull has the reverse color scheme with a dark body and white head.
